assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural methods for estimating demand and competition have transformed empirical industrial organization and policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn are central, identifiable contributors to the core demand and dynamic-industry frameworks.
assessment.maturity: The methods are long established, widely used and have generated extensive applied evidence.
uncertainties: The candidate formulation encompasses several distinct contributions and more major contributors than can receive the prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection supplied a durable organizing framework for modern trade and its welfare implications.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is the clearest focal contributor, with Helpman and Redding important to the wider theoretical development.
assessment.maturity: The framework has been deeply incorporated into trade theory and confronted with substantial firm-level evidence.
uncertainties: Credit for related heterogeneous-firm trade contributions is broader than three individuals.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The analysis of information technology, network effects and digital-market competition has had large and lasting intellectual and policy influence.
assessment.attribution: Shapiro, Varian and Farrell have especially clear links to foundational analysis of network industries and competition.
assessment.maturity: The ideas have shaped decades of scholarship and competition-policy practice.
uncertainties: The discovery label is broad and includes several partially overlapping literatures.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Political-economy models of trade policy gave a coherent account of how organized interests shape protection.
assessment.attribution: Grossman and Helpman are the unambiguous central pair for the stated contribution.
assessment.maturity: The work is mature, canonical and influential across trade and political economy.
uncertainties: The empirical reach of particular political-economy mechanisms varies across settings.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Monopsony has substantially changed understanding of wage setting, employer power and labor-market policy.
assessment.attribution: Manning supplied a foundational modern framework, while Naidu has been important in contemporary theory and evidence.
assessment.maturity: The literature is now central to labor economics and supported by a growing body of empirical work.
uncertainties: The precise boundary between foundational monopsony theory and newer empirical advances remains contestable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantifying misallocation made firm-level distortions a central explanation for productivity and income differences.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow are the clearest focal authors for the influential accounting framework.
assessment.maturity: The contribution has produced a large follow-on literature and sustained empirical application.
uncertainties: Interpretation of measured wedges as policy-relevant distortions is model-dependent.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The combination of selection theory and credible measurement has reshaped empirical insurance economics.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein, Einav and Salanie have each made major contributions linking insurance-market data to asymmetric-information models.
assessment.maturity: The research program is mature and influential in health, public finance and insurance-market design.
uncertainties: The candidate combines foundational theory with a broad empirical literature whose credit is diffuse.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Modern analysis of agglomeration and urban spatial organization has illuminated a major determinant of productivity and living standards.
assessment.attribution: Glaeser, Puga and Duranton are prominent contributors to the theoretical and empirical core.
assessment.maturity: The field has accumulated extensive evidence and has clear relevance to urban and housing policy.
uncertainties: The broad candidate description makes a narrow, three-person attribution difficult.
